claims.text: Conventionally powder-processed W–Cu composites, including those made by spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying, typically suffer from phase separation and void defects.
A short, controlled laser pulse can selectively remelt a vapor-deposited Cu coating on W particles without boiling the Cu.
Localized heating to approximately 1300–1500 °C will melt the Cu interlayer while leaving the W phase solid.
Rapid quenching after laser heating will preserve a fine W–Cu microstructure.
Laser-induced melting of the Cu coating will improve Cu wetting of W surfaces.
The transient Cu liquid phase will promote atomic interdiffusion at W–Cu interfaces.
Improved wetting and interdiffusion will create continuous, well-bonded Cu interphases connecting W particles.
Transient liquid-phase sintering will eliminate or substantially reduce pre-existing interfacial voids and defects.
Interfacial voids and defects impair thermal transport in W–Cu composites.
Interfacial voids and defects impair the mechanical durability of W–Cu composites during service.
The laser-activated composite will have more than 30% lower void content than a conventionally spark-plasma-sintered or mechanically alloyed baseline.
The laser-activated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the conventional baseline.
The laser-activated composite will have greater mechanical robustness under irradiation than the conventional baseline.
Reducing voids and strengthening W–Cu interfaces will preserve heat-transfer efficiency under irradiation.
The proposed method is limited to W-containing composites whose W particles initially possess a vapor-deposited Cu coating.
Excessive thermal gradients or improper laser-pulse parameters may induce residual stresses.
